cards.title: Google Compute Engine (GCE)
cards.teaser: GCE is GCP's IaaS layer — raw virtual machines provisioned on Google's global infrastructure. It is the foundation beneath every higher-level compute service and the right choice whenever you need direct OS control.

runs.text: Google Compute Engine

(GCE) provides Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) virtual machines running on Google's global network of data centers. Unlike managed services such as Cloud Run or App Engine, GCE gives you full control over the operating system, kernel, networking configuration, and storage layout.

A GCE instance is fundamentally a hypervisor-backed VM. Google uses a custom KVM-based hypervisor with hardware accelerators for network and storage I/O. VMs boot from persistent disk images, can attach multiple disk volumes, and communicate over Google's Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.
Launching a minimal VM with the gcloud CLI:
GCE is the correct abstraction when you need:

items.text: — custom kernel modules, specialized system daemons, third-party agents.
— moving existing on-premises workloads to the cloud without re-architecting.
— databases, licensing servers, HPC jobs that require persistent local state.
— GPUs for ML training, high-memory configs for in-memory databases, Local SSDs for latency-sensitive I/O.

runs.text: GKE (Kubernetes Engine), Cloud Run, and Dataproc all run on top of GCE node pools under the hood. Understanding GCE deeply means you understand the substrate of Google's entire managed compute portfolio.

GCE rents you a virtual machine in Google's data center. You control everything about it — the OS, the software, the network rules — but Google handles the physical hardware and the hypervisor underneath.

cards.title: Machine Families
cards.teaser: GCE organizes VM shapes into four machine families — N, C, M, and A — each optimized for a different workload axis: general purpose, compute-intensive, memory-intensive, and accelerator-heavy. Choosing the wrong family wastes money or performance.

runs.text: Google organizes machine types into families that reflect the primary optimization target. Within each family, generations (N1, N2, N2D, N4) track successive hardware generations offering improved price-performance.

items.text: — balanced vCPU-to-memory ratios (1:4 to 1:8 GB/vCPU). N2 uses Intel Cascade/Ice Lake; N2D uses AMD EPYC Rome/Milan; N4 uses Intel Emerald Rapids. Best for: web servers, app servers, development environments, small-to-medium databases. N2D typically offers 20% lower cost than N2 for the same vCPU count.

— highest vCPU clock speeds, low memory ratio (1:2 GB/vCPU). C2 uses Intel Cascade Lake with turbo up to 3.8 GHz; C2D uses AMD EPYC. Best for: compute-bound analytics (BigQuery BI Engine, Spark executors), gaming backends, media encoding, high-frequency trading. When CPU speed matters more than RAM.

— extreme memory per vCPU (up to 1:24 GB/vCPU). M1 offers up to 3.75 TB RAM; M2 ultra reaches 12 TB RAM in a single VM. Best for: in-memory databases (SAP HANA, Redis at scale), large in-memory analytics, ERP systems that cannot be horizontally scaled. The most expensive family — justified only when the entire working set must fit in RAM.

— purpose-built for GPU and TPU workloads. A2 attaches NVIDIA A100 GPUs (up to 16 per VM); A3 attaches NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Best for: ML training (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX), LLM inference, scientific simulation, video rendering. GPU memory bandwidth, not vCPU count, is the primary performance dimension here.

runs.text: A quick decision guide:

items.text: N2 or N2D — covers 80% of workloads.
CPU is the bottleneck, not RAM:
Working set must fit in RAM:

runs.text: Machine type naming follows the pattern family-class-vCPUs. For example, n2-standard-16 is an N2 family, standard sub-type (1:4 vCPU:RAM ratio), with 16 vCPUs and 64 GB RAM. The sub-type variants within a family are: standard (balanced), highmem (more RAM), highcpu (more vCPUs), and megamem / ultramem for extreme memory.

Think of machine families as menu sections: N is the everyday menu (most workloads), C is for when your app is starving for CPU cycles, M is for when your app needs a massive amount of RAM, and A is when you need a GPU for machine learning. Pick the section that matches your bottleneck.

cards.title: Custom Machine Types
cards.teaser: When no predefined shape fits your workload, custom machine types let you specify the exact number of vCPUs and the exact amount of RAM — paying only for what you actually need.

runs.text: Predefined machine types come in fixed vCPU-to-RAM ratios. If your workload needs an unusual combination — say, 12 vCPUs with 48 GB RAM, or 6 vCPUs with 100 GB RAM — you would normally be forced to over-provision one dimension.
Custom machine types solve this. You specify vCPU count and memory independently, within a family's allowed ranges:

explanation.text:
# Create a custom N2 VM: 6 vCPUs, 40 GB RAM
gcloud compute instances create custom-vm \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2-custom-6-40960 \
  --image-family=ubuntu-2204-lts \
  --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud

runs.text: The format is
FAMILY-custom-VCPUS-MEMORY_MB
. Memory must be a multiple of 256 MB. Constraints by family:

items.text: 2–128 vCPUs; 0.5 GB to 8 GB RAM per vCPU; total RAM 1 GB–864 GB.
2–224 vCPUs; 0.5 GB to 8 GB RAM per vCPU.
to push beyond 8 GB RAM per vCPU, at a ~25% premium on the extended memory portion.

runs.text: Pricing for custom types is calculated per vCPU-hour plus per GB-hour of RAM. This is always slightly more expensive than the equivalent predefined type (typically 5–10% premium) but cheaper than the next-size predefined type if you are between sizes.

Custom machine types are not available in the A-series or M-series families. They are supported on N1, N2, N2D, N4, E2, and C2D families. Always verify family support in the GCP docs before designing around custom shapes.

Custom machine types are like ordering a sandwich with exactly the ingredients you want instead of choosing from a preset menu. You specify vCPUs and RAM independently, paying only for that exact combination.

cards.title: Instance Templates
cards.teaser: An instance template is a reusable VM blueprint — it captures machine type, disk image, network config, labels, and metadata in a single versioned resource that managed instance groups use to create identical VMs at scale.

runs.text: Every time you create a VM from scratch, you specify machine type, boot disk, image, network interface, service account, startup script, labels, and metadata. An
instance template
captures all of these in one immutable, globally referenceable resource.

explanation.text:
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-server-template \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-2 \
  --image-family=debian-12 \
  --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --boot-disk-size=30GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-balanced \
  --metadata=startup-script='#!/bin/bash
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx
    systemctl enable --now nginx' \
  --tags=http-server \
  --service-account=web-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

runs.text: Key properties of instance templates:

items.text: To change a template, create a new version with a different name or use managed instance group rolling updates.
A single template can be used by MIGs in any region.
(newer, recommended) support regional persistent disks and are scoped to a single region for tighter governance.
— inline scripts or Cloud Storage references. Executed on first boot.
— point to a hardened gold image instead of a public image family for faster boot and pre-installed software.

runs.text: Without instance templates, managed instance groups cannot create replacement VMs — templates are a hard prerequisite for MIGs, autoscalers, and managed rolling updates.

Version your templates by embedding a date or build number in the name (e.g., web-server-template-20250901). This makes rollbacks straightforward: update the MIG to reference the prior template version.

An instance template is a saved recipe for a VM. Whenever a managed group needs to create a new VM — for scaling or replacing a failed instance — it follows this recipe exactly, ensuring every VM in the group is identical.

cards.title: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs)
cards.teaser: Managed instance groups maintain a fleet of identical VMs using an instance template, providing autoscaling, autohealing, rolling updates, and stateful or stateless operating modes — making them GCE's answer to Kubernetes deployments for VM workloads.

runs.text: A
Managed Instance Group

(MIG) is a collection of VMs that GCE manages as a unit. All instances are created from the same instance template. GCE continuously monitors the group and automatically repairs, replaces, and scales instances.

explanation.text:
# Create a regional MIG with autoscaling
gcloud compute instance-groups managed create web-mig \
  --template=web-server-template \
  --size=3 \
  --region=us-central1

gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --min-num-replicas=2 \
  --max-num-replicas=20 \
  --target-cpu-utilization=0.7 \
  --cool-down-period=90

runs.text: Core MIG capabilities:

items.text: — scale out/in based on CPU utilization, HTTP load balancing serving capacity, Stackdriver metrics, or Cloud Pub/Sub queue depth. Scale-out triggers immediately; scale-in has a stabilization window to prevent thrashing.

— attach an HTTP health check; GCE automatically recreates VMs that fail consecutive health checks. Configurable initial delay (default 300 s) prevents premature replacement of instances that are still booting.

— update to a new template in waves. Configure max surge (extra VMs during rollout) and max unavailable (VMs that can be down simultaneously). Supports canary updates: roll out to N% of instances first.

— stateless MIGs (the default) treat all VMs as fungible. Stateful MIGs preserve per-instance state: assigned persistent disks, static IPs, and instance-specific metadata survive autohealing replacements.
— zonal MIGs deploy to a single zone (lower latency, simpler); regional MIGs spread across 3 zones for higher availability. For production, prefer regional.

runs.text: Stateful MIGs are designed for workloads that are not container-friendly but still need managed lifecycles: legacy Java EE apps, database replicas, VMs with licensed software that tracks the instance identity. The stateful policy explicitly names which disks and network interfaces to preserve across replacements.

A MIG is a self-managing fleet of identical VMs. Tell it the template, the desired size, and the health check — it handles scaling, replacing unhealthy VMs, and rolling out new software versions without any manual intervention.

cards.title: Sole-Tenant Nodes
cards.teaser: Sole-tenant nodes give your VMs dedicated physical hosts, guaranteeing no other customer's workloads share your hardware — required for bring-your-own-license (BYOL) scenarios and certain compliance mandates.

runs.text: By default, GCE VMs are multi-tenant: Google's hypervisor runs VMs from many customers on the same physical server. For most workloads this is fine — the hypervisor enforces strict isolation. But some requirements break multi-tenancy:

items.text: — Windows Server and SQL Server licenses purchased under Microsoft's per-core licensing model require dedicated physical cores to be portable to the cloud. Multi-tenant VMs cannot satisfy this.
— certain government, financial, or healthcare frameworks require physical isolation as a contractual or regulatory requirement.
— some latency-sensitive workloads require guaranteed access to physical CPU without noisy-neighbor effects.

explanation.text:
# Create a sole-tenant node template
gcloud compute sole-tenancy node-templates create sql-node-template \
  --node-type=n2-node-80-640 \
  --region=us-east1

# Create a node group
gcloud compute sole-tenancy node-groups create sql-node-group \
  --node-template=sql-node-template \
  --target-size=2 \
  --zone=us-east1-b

# Create a VM on the sole-tenant node
gcloud compute instances create sql-vm \
  --zone=us-east1-b \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-16 \
  --node-group=sql-node-group \
  --image-family=windows-2022 \
  --image-project=windows-cloud \
  --license-type=windows-server-2022

runs.text: A sole-tenant node is a single physical server with all its resources (vCPUs, RAM) reserved for one customer. You pay for the entire node regardless of how many VMs fill it — so bin-packing your VMs efficiently onto nodes is important for cost control.

Sole-tenant nodes are significantly more expensive than shared-tenancy VMs because you are renting the full physical machine. They are justified only when licensing, compliance, or performance requirements make multi-tenancy impossible — not as a general performance enhancement.

A sole-tenant node is a physical server that Google reserves entirely for you. No other customer's VMs run on it. This costs more, but it is required when your software license says 'dedicated physical cores only' or when your auditors require physical isolation.

cards.title: Spot VMs (Preemptible VMs)
cards.teaser: Spot VMs offer up to 91% discounts over on-demand pricing by running on GCP's spare capacity — GCP can reclaim them with a 30-second warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. The right choice for fault-tolerant batch and ML training jobs.

runs.text: GCP has two names for the same concept: the newer
Spot VM
(no maximum runtime, market-based availability) and the older
Preemptible VM
(24-hour maximum runtime, fixed 60–91% discount). Spot VMs are the current recommendation — they have no 24-hour cap, but may be harder to acquire during high-demand periods.

explanation.text:
# Create a Spot VM
gcloud compute instances create batch-worker \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-8 \
  --image-family=debian-12 \
  --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --provisioning-model=SPOT \
  --instance-termination-action=STOP

# Create a preemptible VM (legacy flag)
gcloud compute instances create batch-worker-v1 \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-8 \
  --preemptible

runs.text: What happens when GCP reclaims a Spot VM:

items.text: via the ACPI G2 soft off signal and a metadata server value change at
. Applications can poll the metadata server or register a shutdown hook.
— STOP (default) halts the VM preserving disk; DELETE removes the VM entirely. For batch jobs, STOP allows resuming from last checkpoint.
— configure a MIG to use Spot VMs with a fallback to on-demand if no spot capacity is available. The MIG will automatically replace reclaimed VMs.

runs.text: Best workloads for Spot VMs: large-scale ML training (with checkpointing), Dataproc Spark jobs, video transcoding pipelines, Monte Carlo simulations, genomics batch processing. Worst fit: production web servers, databases, anything without checkpointing.

For ML training on A2 or A3 instances, Spot VMs can reduce GPU hour costs from $3.67/hr (A100 on-demand) to under $1.10/hr — a saving of 70%+. Frameworks like JAX and PyTorch support checkpoint-and-restore natively, making spot-based training practical for large models.

A Spot VM is like a standby seat on a flight — much cheaper, but the airline can bump you if they need the seat for a full-fare passenger. Your job must be able to checkpoint and resume, but the cost savings are dramatic.

cards.title: Sustained-Use Discounts
cards.teaser: Sustained-use discounts (SUDs) are automatic, incremental credits that GCP applies to on-demand VMs the longer they run within a calendar month — no commitment or sign-up required.

runs.text: Sustained-use discounts reward steady, long-running workloads automatically. GCP tracks how many vCPU and memory hours you consume each calendar month and applies tiered discounts with no user action required.
The discount tiers for N1, N2, and N2D general-purpose machine types:
A VM that runs 100% of the month effectively receives ~30% discount on the total bill compared to per-hour on-demand pricing. This is the blended effective rate across all four tiers.
Important limitations:

items.text: SUDs apply per region, not globally.
GCP aggregates vCPUs and memory usage within a region and combines hours across instances of the same machine type family.
E2, N1, N2, N2D, C2, and C2D families receive SUDs. A2, M1, M2, and Spot VMs do not.
Committed-use discounts and SUDs do not stack.
CUD hours are excluded from SUD calculations — committed resources are already discounted.

runs.text: If your workload runs more than 25% of the month, SUDs automatically kick in. For steady 24/7 services — monitoring agents, always-on APIs, persistent workers — you get meaningful savings with zero operational effort. SUDs are the reason GCP's effective compute costs often compare favorably to AWS on-demand even without reserved instances.
Sustained-use discounts are like a loyalty reward that accrues automatically. The longer your VM runs in a month, the cheaper each additional hour becomes — no contracts, no upfront commitments.

cards.title: Committed-Use Discounts (CUDs)
cards.teaser: Committed-use discounts (CUDs) offer up to 70% savings in exchange for a 1- or 3-year usage commitment. Resource-based CUDs lock in a specific machine type; flex CUDs cover any machine type in a family, giving you flexibility as workloads evolve.

runs.text: Committed-use discounts are GCP's equivalent of AWS Reserved Instances and Azure Reserved VM Instances. You commit to a minimum usage level for 1 or 3 years in exchange for a significant discount over on-demand pricing.
There are two CUD types:

items.text: — commit to a specific vCPU and memory amount within a region, regardless of which specific machine type you use. All N2 vCPUs in us-central1, for example. Discounts: 37% for 1 year, 55% for 3 years on general-purpose families.

— commit to a minimum hourly spend (in dollars) on a machine family in a region. GCP applies the discount to any machine type within that family, including custom machine types. Flex CUDs apply automatically as you use resources — no per-VM assignment required. Discounts are slightly lower than resource-based CUDs (~28% for 1 year on N2).

runs.text: CUD math for a production service with 20 n2-standard-8 VMs running 24/7 in us-central1:

explanation.text:
# Purchase a 1-year resource-based CUD for N2 in us-central1
gcloud compute commitments create my-n2-commitment \
  --plan=12-month \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --resources=vcpu=160,memory=640GB \
  --type=GENERAL_PURPOSE_N2

runs.text: Flex CUDs vs resource CUDs: use flex CUDs when your machine type mix is expected to change (e.g., as you migrate from N2 to N4). Use resource CUDs when the workload is stable and you want maximum discount.

CUD commitments are binding — you are billed for the committed amount even if you run fewer resources. Model your steady-state baseline carefully and commit only to that floor. Use on-demand or spot VMs for burst capacity above the committed level.

CUDs are like a gym membership: you pay a flat monthly fee for guaranteed access at a lower per-use rate. Resource CUDs lock you to a specific type of machine; flex CUDs let you use any machine in the family. Both save money only if you actually use what you commit to.

cards.title: Live Migration
cards.teaser: GCE live migration transparently moves a running VM from one physical host to another during host maintenance — without a reboot, without a restart, and without the VM even noticing beyond a brief CPU slowdown.

runs.text: Google operates a global fleet of physical servers that requires periodic hardware maintenance: firmware updates, hardware repairs, memory replacement, kernel patching of the host OS. On most cloud providers, this means a VM reboot. On GCE, it means
live migration
— the VM is moved to a different physical host while it is still running.
How live migration works:

items.text: — GCE iteratively copies dirty memory pages from the source host to the destination host while the VM continues running. Multiple rounds of copy reduce the divergence between source and destination.
— once dirty page rate is low enough, GCE briefly pauses the VM (typically < 250 ms), copies the remaining state, and resumes execution on the destination host.
— VPC network flows are transparently redirected to the new host. The VM's IP address and MAC address are unchanged.

runs.text: From the VM's perspective, live migration appears as a brief slowdown (2–4 seconds of elevated latency during pre-copy) and a ~250 ms pause. The application continues running; TCP connections are not dropped.
Exceptions — VMs that cannot be live-migrated:

items.text: VMs with GPUs or Local SSDs
— the hardware is physically attached to the host. These VMs receive a host maintenance notification and are terminated (and can be configured to restart automatically).
— live migration is not performed; the VM is preempted.

runs.text: Live migration is the reason GCE's uptime SLA can reach 99.99% for VMs configured with automatic restart and on a single zone. Compare to cloud providers where host maintenance windows require planned downtime — live migration eliminates that category of outage entirely.

Live migration is like moving a sleeping person from one bed to another without waking them. GCE copies your VM's memory to a new physical host in the background, then silently switches over — your applications keep running throughout.

cards.title: Local SSD
cards.teaser: Local SSDs are NVMe flash drives physically attached to the VM's host server — offering up to 2.4 million IOPS and sub-millisecond latency, at the cost of being ephemeral: the data is lost when the VM stops or is terminated.

runs.text: Persistent disks (pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd) are network-attached block storage — durable, replicable, snapshotable, but limited by network bandwidth.
Local SSDs
bypass the network entirely: the NVMe flash is mounted directly to the physical host running your VM.
Performance characteristics:

items.text: 375 GB per local SSD partition; attach up to 24 per VM for 9 TB total.
Up to 2,400 MB/s sequential read; 1,200 MB/s sequential write.
Up to 2.4 million random read IOPS; 1.2 million random write IOPS (across all attached local SSDs).
Typically 50–100 microseconds, compared to 1–3 ms for pd-ssd.

explanation.text:
# Create a VM with 2 local SSD partitions (750 GB total)
gcloud compute instances create fast-cache-vm \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-16 \
  --image-family=debian-12 \
  --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --local-ssd=interface=NVME \
  --local-ssd=interface=NVME

runs.text: Ephemeral trade-off: local SSD data is lost when the VM is stopped, deleted, or live-migrated (GPUs + local SSDs get terminated, not migrated). This makes local SSD appropriate only for:

items.text: Scratch space and temporary working sets
— Spark shuffle data, sort buffers, video encode scratch.
— Redis cache, memcached, write-through caches where loss means a cold cache, not data loss.
— ML batch inference where intermediate state is regenerated from input data.

runs.text: Never use local SSD as the sole copy of important data. If your VM is terminated (spot reclaim, host failure, accidental deletion), the data is gone. Use local SSD as a fast scratch layer with durable persistence backed by pd-ssd or Cloud Storage.

Local SSD is incredibly fast because the drive is inside the same physical server as your VM — there is no network hop. The trade-off is that it disappears when the VM stops. Treat it like RAM: fast, temporary, and worthless without a backup layer.

cards.title: Custom Images
cards.teaser: Custom images — also called gold images or golden images — are pre-configured, hardened VM disk snapshots that serve as the base for all instances in your fleet, eliminating per-boot provisioning time and enforcing a consistent security baseline.

runs.text: Starting from a public image (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04) and running a startup script on every VM boot is the simplest approach but has two costs: boot time (installing packages, configuring agents) and configuration drift (startup script logic changes may not apply consistently).
Custom images
solve both by baking all configuration into the disk image before any VM is launched.
The typical custom image workflow:

items.text: — Debian, Ubuntu, COS (Container-Optimized OS), or Windows Server.
— install agents (Ops Agent, security tools, monitoring daemons), apply OS hardening (CIS benchmarks, SSH key restrictions, audit rules), install your runtime (JDK, Node.js, Python).
Stop the VM and create the image
— GCE takes a snapshot of the boot disk.
— group images in a family (e.g., corp-debian12-hardened); the latest image in the family is the active default.

explanation.text:
# Create a custom image from a stopped instance's boot disk
gcloud compute images create corp-debian12-v20250901 \
  --source-disk=provisioned-vm \
  --source-disk-zone=us-central1-a \
  --family=corp-debian12-hardened \
  --labels=env=production,os=debian,version=12 \
  --storage-location=us

# Use the image family in an instance template
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-template \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-2 \
  --image-family=corp-debian12-hardened \
  --image-project=my-project

runs.text: Tools like Packer (HashiCorp) automate the build-provision-capture cycle, enabling image-as-code pipelines where a code change to the image definition triggers a CI build that produces a new image version.

Custom images compress VM boot time from minutes (startup script + package install) to seconds (everything pre-installed). For MIGs that autoscale rapidly under load — a flash sale traffic spike, a sudden batch job burst — the difference between a 30-second boot and a 3-minute boot determines whether autoscaling helps before the peak passes.

A custom image is a fully prepared disk snapshot you create once and reuse thousands of times. Instead of every new VM installing software from scratch, it boots from your pre-configured snapshot and is ready in seconds.

cards.title: Shielded VMs
cards.teaser: Shielded VMs add a hardware-rooted security layer to GCE instances — secure boot, a virtual TPM, and integrity monitoring — to defend against rootkits, bootkit malware, and unauthorized firmware modifications.

runs.text: A standard VM boots from a disk image and trusts that the bootloader, kernel, and early OS are intact. An attacker with access to the boot disk — or the ability to modify UEFI firmware — could inject malicious code that persists invisibly below the OS.
Shielded VMs
address this threat model with three interlocking controls.

items.text: — enforces that only software signed by trusted keys (Google, Microsoft, or your own CA) can execute during the boot process. Bootloaders and kernel modules that lack valid signatures are rejected before they can run. Prevents bootkits and UEFI-level persistence.

— a software-emulated TPM 2.0 device. The vTPM measures and seals the boot sequence into Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs). Enables cryptographic attestation: you can verify remotely that a VM booted from an expected state. Also provides a secure key store for applications.

— compares the current boot measurements against a known-good baseline. If the measured boot differs from the baseline (e.g., a kernel module was changed), GCE logs the deviation to Cloud Monitoring and can alert on it. The baseline is updated whenever you intentionally change the boot configuration.

explanation.text:
# Create a Shielded VM
gcloud compute instances create secure-vm \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2-standard-4 \
  --image-family=debian-12 \
  --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --shielded-secure-boot \
  --shielded-vtpm \
  --shielded-integrity-monitoring

# Verify shielded VM policy on the project
gcloud compute project-info describe \
  --format='value(defaultServiceAccount)'

runs.text: Shielded VMs require a Shielded VM-compatible OS image. Most Google-provided images (Debian, Ubuntu, COS, Windows Server 2019+) support Shielded VM. Custom images must also be built from a Shielded-compatible base and have the Shielded VM flag set.
Shielded VMs are relevant for:

items.text: — FedRAMP High, PCI DSS, and NIST SP 800-53 reference controls that require boot integrity verification.
— VMs handling cryptographic keys, customer PII, or financial transactions where persistent rootkits represent a catastrophic risk.

— the vTPM enables Workload Identity Federation: a VM can cryptographically prove to external systems (e.g., a secrets manager, an on-premises API) that it is the expected VM before receiving credentials.

runs.text: Enabling Shielded VM has negligible performance impact — the measurement and attestation happen at boot time, not during runtime. There is no reason not to enable it for any VM handling sensitive data. GCP's own Confidential Computing VMs build on Shielded VM by also encrypting RAM in use.

A Shielded VM verifies its own identity every time it boots: it checks that the bootloader, kernel, and firmware have not been tampered with. If something changed unexpectedly, it reports the deviation before the VM even starts handling traffic.
